Overview
Pedal puncture wounds are common, and infection occurs in as many as 10% of
patients.1 Osteomyelitis occurs in 1.8% of patients and may result in loss of limb.2
Tetanus immunization status should be confirmed and updated. Antibiotic prophylaxis is
indicated in all patients except those with a clean, superficial pedal puncture wound and
no retained foreign material who seek treatment within 24 hours postinjury. Metallic
foreign bodies do not need to be routinely removed.
Plain radiographs should be obtained in all patients with a pedal puncture wound.3
Advanced imaging studies are utilized to evaluate for radiolucent foreign material,
adjacent structure injury, or osteomyelitis. Deeper infections should be managed
appropriately via surgical treatment and parenteral antibiotic agents. Patients with
diabetes mellitus require special consideration because of higher complication rates,
including a 46-fold increased risk of amputation postinjury.4

Patient History and Physical Examination
A thoughtful patient history is critical in evaluating a pedal puncture wound. For a more
acute injury, the most important factors to ascertain are the timing of the injury and
whether the patient was shod or unshod at the time of injury. If the patient was shod,
the physician should inquire about the type of shoe, its materials, and any damage to
the shoe at the puncture site because softer shoe material may have been injected into
the puncture wound track. At a minimum, Pseudomonas species that colonized the shoe
may have inoculated the puncture site, requiring antibiotic treatment. The physician also
should inquire about interventions attempted or observations made before the patient
sought definitive medical evaluation and treatment. These include the circumstances of
the injury; the surrounding environment; the amount and severity of initial bleeding;
and, most importantly, the nature of any material removed from the foot at the time.
These observations may increase the suspicion of retained foreign material and alter
antimicrobial management.
Particular attention should be given to puncture wounds in patients with diabetes
mellitus. In patients with diabetes mellitus, tetanus is three times more likely,5 infections
resulting from puncture wounds are more likely to progress to osteomyelitis and are
more likely to be polymicrobial, and the risk of amputation is 46 times higher than in
other patients.4 Patients with a history of systemic inflammatory or other autoimmune
conditions, peripheral vascular disease, or any immunocompromised state may have the
same degree of morbidity as patients with diabetes mellitus.
The physical examination begins with identification of the zone of the puncture wound.
Three zones have been described. Zone 1 is distal to the metatarsal neck, zone 2
encompasses the transverse tarsal joint to the metatarsal neck, and zone 3 is the
calcaneus or heel region. Of the 3% to 10% of pedal puncture wounds that result in

thorough cleaning of the site. Macerated skin margins may harbor bacteria and
predispose the patient to later infectious complications. If possible, the depth of the
puncture wound should be assessed. The patient also should be assessed for any
tendon or nerve injury.7

Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs should be considered the minimum diagnostic imaging study for the
evaluation of a pedal puncture wound in a patient in whom a foreign body is suspected,
including suspected glass. A common misconception is that glass must contain lead to
be radiopaque. Glass may be identified on plain radiographs because it is denser than
the surrounding soft tissue not because of any particular chemical additives, such as
lead. A radiopaque foreign body is present in 15% of patients.8 If an acute puncture
wound is evaluated in the emergency department or office setting and a normal plain
radiograph leads to a low index of suspicion of a foreign body, then it is reasonable to
complete the puncture wound treatment algorithm and defer additional imaging
studies;9 however, foreign bodies are missed on initial evaluation of approximately one-
third of puncture wounds.10 If a foreign body is suspected in a patient with a puncture
wound but is not observed on plain radiographs (85% incidence), then advanced imaging
studies are recommended.
Ultrasonography is an inexpensive and widely available imaging modality that can
accurately identity superficial radiolucent foreign bodies without exposing the patient to
ionizing radiation.11 A high-frequency (7.5 MHz or higher) linear array transducer is ideal
for identifying suspected foreign material in the musculoskeletal system. Although
echogenicity is related to the material properties of the foreign body, foreign bodies in
the extremities typically demonstrate hyperechogenicity. If the foreign body is
associated with an inflammatory response or granulation tissue, a hypoechoic rim may
be observed around the foreign body. These areas show hypervascularity on power

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000501
6/23

Doppler ultrasonography and can be detected as early as 24 hours postinjury.12,13
Ultrasonographic artifacts also can be detected. Smooth or clean shadowing or rough or
dirty shadowing may reveal the depth of the foreign body and depend on its shape
rather than its material properties. Gas also may be detected as a reverberation artifact
and may be consistent with an acute puncture wound or the presence of gas-forming
bacteria and necrotic infection.14
Ultrasonography can identify adjacent soft-tissue injury and is the best imaging modality
to detect the presence of wood in patients with a pedal puncture wound.
Ultrasonography can be used to localize a foreign body and aid in removal via a
technique known as hydrodissection. Local anesthesia is injected, and the encapsulating
granulation tissue is separated from the foreign body, facilitating its removal.
The role of CT in detecting foreign bodies in the musculoskeletal system is limited. The
precise location of a radiopaque foreign body can be determined via CT; however, the
diagnostic value of CT is limited if radiolucent material is suspected. Materials such as
wood appear moderately hyperattenuating on CT scans and may be identified.8 Glass is
more easily identified on CT scans. At a density of 2,000 HU, a minimum volume of 0.07
mm3 was observed via 16-multidetector CT. CT scans can show the presence of air or gas
and help identify abnormalities in adjacent structures.15 Placement of stereotactic
needles via CT localization may make the removal of a radiopaque foreign body easier;
however, this technique is of limited benefit in patients with a pedal puncture wound
because intraoperative orthogonal radiographs are more easily obtained.
MRI has a minimal role in the evaluation of acute pedal puncture wounds; however, MRI
(3-Tesla MRI, or contrast-enhanced MRI if 3-Tesla MRI is not medically acceptable) is
indicated and is the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of a delayed, chronic,
long-standing, or complicated puncture wound in patients with or without a foreign
body.16 If the delay between the puncture wound and patient presentation is
substantial, patients may not recall a puncture wound or may not mention it, assuming
that it was a minor, resolved, and irrelevant incident not related to the current concern.
For chronic injuries, MRI is particularly useful to identify an abscess, a sinus tract,
infectious tenosynovitis, and osteomyelitis. Evaluation via plain radiographs is common
in patients with foot pain. A radiopaque foreign body, particularly a metallic foreign
body, should be evident, and the complications of exposing metallic material to a large
magnetic field always must be considered and avoided. Those complications include

In the absence of a puncture wound history, MRI may be misleading. The differential
diagnosis for commonly observed well-encapsulated multiloculated cystic masses
includes seroma, liquefied hematoma, cold abscess, or cystic degeneration within a soft-
tissue sarcoma. A sinus tract with enhancing walls may be evident on contrast-enhanced,
T1-weighted, fat-suppressed MRIs. MRI features that suggest a foreign body granuloma
include susceptibility artifact and a hypointense rim on T2-weighted MRIs. Even contrast-
enhanced MRI may be insufficient to differentiate tumors from masses associated with a
foreign body.17


Pedal Puncture Wound Inoculation Injury
The common pathophysiologic pathway for infection of pedal puncture wounds is
inoculation with skin flora or surface contamination with the offending foreign material.
The energy and trauma of the puncture wound may inject shoe material or lead to
retention of a foreign body.
Granuloma formation occurs in response to retained foreign material via a process of
granulomatous inflammation. This is a type of chronic inflammation that occurs in
response to cellular injury and mediator release, resulting in histocytes, fibroblasts, and
angiogenesis. These immature cells organize, coalesce, and wall off the foreign material.
Delayed presentation of organic radiolucent foreign material in patients who do not
recall a pedal puncture wound may present a difficult diagnostic scenario based on
imaging findings, particularly if adjacent bone is involved. Differential diagnoses include
neoplasm, osteoid osteoma, chronic or acute osteomyelitis, tuberculosis granuloma,
bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst, and fibrous cortical defect.18
Infectious complication is related to time delay from injury to patient presentation,
bacterial load/contamination of the skin or foreign material, location/zone of the
puncture, degree of energy of the puncture, and host factors. The body’s reaction to the
foreign material depends, in part, on the material itself.
Retained glass is present after a puncture wound in 9% to 24% of patients.19 The
sharper edges of glass tend to penetrate deeper and may cause injury to tendons,
ligaments, or neurovascular structures near a puncture site. Glass is not known to
harbor any unique microorganisms; therefore, antimicrobial prophylaxis and
management should be based on wound, site, and host factors. Glass does not cause
unique inflammatory responses but can migrate in the soft tissue.20 All forms of glass
may be radiopaque.
Wood or other organic material present after a pedal puncture wound may pose a
unique diagnostic challenge because it is radiolucent. Ultrasonography remains the
preferred diagnostic imaging modality to identify organic materials. Wood is an organic
material with layers or interstices of fibrous material. If the wood is older, air is present
between these layers. In addition, dry wood will swell over time, absorbing the
surrounding fluid produced during the body’s response to injury. Organic foreign
material is more likely to contain bacteria, result in an inflammatory response, and result
in infection.8

Pressure-treated wood is one of the more common materials involved in a pedal
puncture wound because of its common use in outdoor locations with high foot traffic,
such as decks. The incidence also is high because softer woods that are prone to
splinter, such as pine, frequently are used to manufacture pressure-treated lumber.
The use of more caustic and toxic chemicals, such as chromated copper arsenate, was
banned by the US Environmental Protection Agency in 2009. Currently, wood is treated
with quaternary ammonium compounds and alkaline copper, which are less toxic. The
main concern related to these chemical additives has been environmental, and concerns
have been raised about inhalation of larger volumes of aerosolized (sawdust or
combustion vapor) pressure-treated wood. Because most pedal puncture wounds result
from small-volume pressure-treated wood (eg, splinter), toxicity because of chemical
leaching is not a principal concern. These injuries are evaluated and managed in the
same manner as other pedal puncture wounds caused by organic materials.
All manner and type of metallic objects have been described as retained foreign bodies
after a pedal puncture wound. Most do not need to be routinely removed because they
are not proinflammatory and the body typically encapsulates them with dense fibrotic
tissue, rendering them clinically inert and asymptomatic13 (Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5,
and Figure 6).

If a retained metallic foreign body is present, MRI can be performed but should be
approved by an attending radiologist on a case-by-case basis. The size, shape, depth,
and relative susceptibility to magnetism (ferromagnetism) of the foreign body are
important details to consider. Ferromagnetic foreign bodies closer to the skin may cause
thermal injury, whereas deeper tissue is potentially protective and may act as a heat
sink. Small objects close to vessels increase the risk of embolism. Long, curved
ferromagnetic (even mildly ferromagnetic) objects have an induced electrical current
from the gradient field and may cause substantial heating if gradients are strong. A
magnetometer may be used in some circumstances to evaluate the ferromagnetism of
foreign bodies before MRI; however, if any safety concerns remain, then removal of an
otherwise asymptomatic metallic foreign body after a pedal puncture wound may be
indicated.

Tetanus Prophylaxis
Tetanus vaccination has been recommended since 1962, when puncture wounds
associated with Clostridium infection were first reported.21 Tetanus vaccines typically are
combined with pertussis and diphtheria vaccines. A tetanus series consists of a
minimum of three doses of tetanus- and diphtheria-containing vaccines. These include
DTap, DTP, Tdap, DT, and Td. The lowercase letters “d” and “p” are used if the
concentration of diphtheria toxoid and pertussis antigen is smaller than that of tetanus.
The letters “ap” refer to acellular pertussis. Age-appropriate vaccines include DTaP for
infants and children aged 6 weeks to 7 years and Td for children aged 7 to 9 years and
adults 65 years and older. Tdap is indicated for patients aged 10 to 64 years. Tetanus
immune globulin is not recommended for infants younger than 6 weeks, and no vaccines
have been approved or licensed by the FDA for this age group. The Tdap vaccine is
administered during pregnancy to prevent pertussis in newborns. Pregnancy is not a
contraindication to tetanus prophylaxis in patients with a puncture wound. The most
common adverse effect is injection site irritation; however, severe encephalitis has been
reported.22

Antibiotic Prophylaxis for Common Organisms
Patients seeking treatment between 24 and 72 hours after a pedal puncture wound
should be administered an oral cephalosporin or dicloxacillin if otherwise asymptomatic.
If infection is present, initial management consists of oral antibiotic agents. If no
improvement occurs within 48 hours, then parenteral antibiotic agents are initiated.
Staphylococcal species are ubiquitous and are the most common organisms that lead to
infection after a pedal puncture wound.23 They are divided into coagulase-positive and
coagulase-negative species. S aureus is coagulase positive and is the most infectious. At
least 30% of individuals are carriers, and, more strikingly, a 24% prevalence of
methicillin-resistant S aureus has been reported.24 Coagulase-negative staphylococcal
species generally are of low virulence and considered a contaminant. If isolated from
multiple broth cultures or from a deep wound culture, they should be considered a
pathogen and managed.
S pyogenes (Group A) and S agalactiae (Group B) also are common organisms and are the
second most common organisms isolated from infected pedal puncture wounds. The
recurrence rate of streptococcal infection is higher in patients with venous stasis.
For staphylococcal and streptococcal species, an oral first-generation cephalosporin
(cephalexin or cefadroxil) can be used for prophylaxis in patients with higher-risk
injuries, in asymptomatic patients 24 to 72 hours postinjury, or as empiric treatment in
patients in whom a superficial infection is suspected. Clindamycin also is appropriate in
this setting. Ampicillin-sulbactam can be used if broader coverage is necessary, with the
potential to add clindamycin. For a deep infection from methicillin-sensitive organisms,
nafcillin is the most effective parenteral antibiotic agent. For methicillin-resistant
infections, vancomycin or linezolid is indicated. If a more serious infection is present,
rifampin can be added for the synergistic effect of this additional antimicrobial.
P aeruginosa is an encapsulated gram-negative rod that can live in soil, in water, or on
nearly any surface, including skin. It is not as virulent as staphylococcal or streptococcal
species but can form biofilms that contribute to rapid antibiotic resistance. Ceftazidime
and aztreonam are the preferred intravenous antibiotic agents for pseudomonal
coverage.
For pedal puncture wounds that occurred underwater, inoculation with aquatic
microorganisms, such as Mycobacterium marinum, Vibrio species, and
Aeromonashydrophila, should be considered and prophylactic antibiotic agentsSEND FEEDBACK

Special Considerations
Osteomyelitis is a rare complication of a pedal puncture wound. Advanced imaging
studies can not only detect radiolucent foreign material but also can be used to evaluate
for osteomyelitis. If osteomyelitis is present, management should consist of surgery and
intravenous antimicrobial agents, the duration of which depends on the degree of
surgical resection and host factors. First described as a cause of pedal puncture wound

infections in 1968,26Pseudomonas species are the most common offending organisms;
however, Klebsiella, Mycobacterium, Eikenella, Enterobacter, Fusobacterium, Proteus, and
Escherichia species have been isolated.2Pseudomonas can form biofilms that contribute
to rapid antibiotic resistance. Empiric management for osteomyelitis includes
ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin, which have the same oral and intravenous efficacy.
Ceftazidime and aztreonam are preferred intravenous antibiotic agents for
pseudomonal coverage.
Pedal puncture wounds in patients with diabetes mellitus require special consideration.
Tetanus infection is three times more common, and mortality is four times more likely.5
No role for observational management exists without antibiotic prophylaxis. Because
these injuries are more likely to result in a polymicrobial infection, a broader-spectrum
oral antimicrobial agent or a combination of antibiotic agents, such as amoxicillin and
clavulanic acid, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or clindamycin and ciprofloxacin, should
be considered. Foreign material, whether radiopaque or radiolucent, identified via
advanced imaging studies, should be removed. Patients with diabetes mellitus require
close follow-up after a pedal puncture wound because they have a much higher risk for
deep infection, osteomyelitis, and loss of limb. For hospitalized patients with diabetes
mellitus, empiric antimicrobial agents, such as piperacillin-tazobactam or imipenem-
cilastatin, are initiated until deep wound cultures are available. Adjunctive treatment
options, such as hyperbaric oxygen, are indicated in patients with diabetes mellitus who
have osteomyelitis (Figure 8).

Management Summary
After a detailed patient history is obtained and a physical examination is performed for a
pedal puncture wound, plain radiographs should be obtained to exclude the presence of
a foreign body. Additional imaging recommendations should be based on the index of
suspicion of retained foreign material.
Tetanus vaccination history should be determined, and appropriate immunization
should be administered. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not universally indicated for pedal
puncture wounds if patient presentation is within 24 hours postinjury; follow-up should
occur within 48 hours. Prophylaxis should be considered in patients with delayed
presentation, higher-energy injuries, wounds with retained foreign material, and factors
such as diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression.
The injured foot should be washed with the use of a diluted povidone-iodine solution;
open chlorhexidine solutions should be avoided because of the risk of Pseudomonas
contamination.27 Macerated skin margins should be cleansed and débrided. Routine
deeper wound exploration can further contaminate and traumatize the foot and
increase infection risk and, therefore, is not indicated. If a retained foreign object,
deeper tissue abscess, infectious tenosynovitis, or osteomyelitis is suspected,
exploration and débridement are indicated. Traumatic or débrided wounds are not
closed; however, if the tissues are incised beyond the wound, these extensions can be
closed with the use of wide nylon sutures.
In most patients, infection can be managed via a 48-hour trial of oral antimicrobial
agents before intravenous antibiotic agents are considered. Additional evaluation and
imaging studies with potential removal of retained foreign material depends on the
